idiom_name: CASL ability built per request from the user's roles (AbilityBuilder + can()) checked with ability.can(action, subject); node-casbin or accesscontrol for table models
implementation_notes: In JavaScript the decision is a value, not an inheritance hierarchy: build an ability for the authenticated user - const { can, build } = new AbilityBuilder(Ability); if (user.roles.includes('editor')) can('update', 'Article', { authorId: user.id }) - and ask it, ability.can(action, subject), at the boundary. CASL assembles permissions into the ability from role data and supports attribute conditions (ownership, tenant) that pure role checks cannot express; rebuild the ability per request from server-side role data, never from a client payload. When the policy is better expressed as a table, node-casbin mirrors the model file (Enforce(sub, obj, act) from model.conf/policy.csv) and the onury accesscontrol package gives a chainable RBAC+ABAC engine with role inheritance and deny-overrides. Enforcement lives in one place - an Express/Koa middleware, a Nest guard (see TypeScript), or a service-layer check - so a route cannot forget it, and the ability's default (empty builder) is already deny.
pitfalls: Roles read from req.body, a query parameter or a client-supplied claim let the caller widen its own permissions; derive the ability from server-side role data.
An ability built once at startup never reflects a revoked role; rebuild it per request (or invalidate on change).
Calling ability.can(action, 'Article') without the subject instance skips attribute conditions, so can('update','Article',{authorId}) is ignored and every editor passes.
Forgetting the enforcement call on one route is invisible at runtime; prefer a single middleware/guard over per-handler checks and test that an unguarded route is denied.
Passing a bare string as the subject loses CASL's condition evaluation; pass subject('Article', article) so the fields are available.
